passages.text: Virtue depends partly upon training and partly upon practice; you must learn first, and then strengthen your learning by action.
passages.note: Growth needs both learning and practice

passages.text: There is no word which reaches our ears without doing us harm; we are injured both by good wishes and by curses. The angry prayers of our enemies instil false fears in us; and the affection of our friends spoils us through their kindly wishes. For this affection sets us a-groping after goods that are far away, unsure, and wavering, when we really might open the store of happiness at home.
passages.note: Others' expectations pull us from contentment

passages.text: “You need not be envious of those whom the people call great and fortunate; applause need not disturb your composed attitude and your sanity of mind; you need not become disgusted with your calm spirit because you see a great man, clothed in purple, protected by the well-known symbols of authority; you need not judge the magistrate for whom the road is cleared to be any happier than yourself, whom his officer pushes from the road. If you would wield a command that is profitable to yourself, and injurious to nobody, clear your own faults out of the way.
passages.note: Envy of the successful and powerful

passages.text: You need never believe that a man can become happy through the unhappiness of another.
passages.note: Happiness cannot come from harming others

passages.text: It is a great part of health to have forsaken the counsellors of madness and to have fled far from a companionship that is mutually baneful.
You can make us cease to crave, if you only make us cease to display. Ambition, luxury, and waywardness need a stage to act upon; you will cure all those ills if you seek retirement.
passages.note: Craving fed by the need to be seen
